balance.argument_a: The induction proof (D1) is airtight for every hierarchy depth Meterworks will ever have. If the target runtime honors tail-call optimization, the real Go-benchmark-anchored cost gap at the Shallow depth is only 0.333 ms vs. 0.164 ms per 10,000 rollups (S1) -- a real but modest 50.8% difference -- making the correctness guarantee nearly free at the depths (up to 5 levels, S5) Meterworks actually has today.
balance.argument_b: Its per-call cost (0.164 ms/10,000 rollups at Shallow, S1) never depends on a runtime detail Devon does not control. Under Go -- the case's actual named target, which does not honor TCO (S4) -- the recursive version costs 3.94 ms/10,000 at the same depth, a real, sourced 95.8% gap, and the real extreme-case benchmark (S2) shows non-tail-callable recursion can reach a ~8.8-million-times gap at depth 40. Meterworks has already shipped one production bug of exactly the shape a real, documented 2022 postmortem describes (S3, -67,343 vs +67,329 on the same account).
balance.margin_basis: Once Appendix D is sourced, compute each option's ms/10,000-rollups at all three hierarchy depths under both TCO scenarios, then compare against Appendix A's latency SLA. The margin is the percent difference between the two options' cost at the depth closest to Appendix A's stated maximum real-world hierarchy depth, under the TCO scenario matching Appendix B's cited fact about the actual named target runtime.
balance.margin_note: COMPUTED 2026-09-01 (case-research). Appendix A's max real-world hierarchy depth is 5 levels (S5); of Appendix D's three depths (Shallow=n10, Medium=n25, Deep=n40), Shallow is closest -- and Shallow is 100% directly-measured data (S1), not a Modeling Assumption. Appendix B's TCO fact (Go does not honor TCO, S4) plus MA7 (target runtime = Go) selects the TCO-not-honored column. At Shallow: Option A (recursive, TCO-not-honored) = 3.94 ms/10,000; Option B (iterative) = 0.164 ms/10,000. margin_pct = (3.94-0.164)/3.94 x 100 = 95.8%. WINNER: Option B, The Guaranteed Floor (iterative). THIS MARGIN IS WIDE, WELL PAST SPEC §2's ~20% cap, AND IS NOT SOFTENED -- reporting it plainly per explicit instruction. Counterfactual check (does MA7 flipping change the story?): under a TCO-honoring runtime, same Shallow row, Option A (TCO-honored) = 0.333 ms/10,000 vs Option B = 0.164 ms/10,000 -> margin = (0.333-0.164)/0.333 = 50.8%. Still far over 20%. So the case's D4 numeric race is NOT close under either runtime -- iterative is genuinely, substantially faster at every measured depth in both real benchmarks (S1, S2), including the TCO-honored column. This is a real finding, not an artifact of a bad assumption: no Modeling Assumption here is a lever that would bring margin_pct under ~20% without contradicting real cited data. The case's actual balance therefore rests on the QUALITATIVE tension already drafted in argument_a/argument_b -- D1's permanent, depth-independent correctness guarantee vs. D4's decisive, real, sourced performance cost -- not on a close numeric race. Recommend case-qa treat this as a disclosed, deliberate lopsided-margin case (like a T1-tier decisive case) rather than attempt a retune, since retuning would require altering S1/S2's real measured ns/op figures, which SPEC §5 forbids.

balance_test_waiver.reason: Per MCS-46: the margin (95.8% at Shallow depth, under Go/non-TCO, the case's actual named target runtime) is real, honestly researched, and structurally driven by the real Go-benchmark-anchored (S1) cost of naive non-tail-callable recursion versus an iterative rewrite, not a modeling shortcut. Waived because (1) the setup still forces genuine multi-step proof work -- constructing and defending the induction proof for the recursive option (base case, inductive step, generalization across every account-hierarchy depth) against the iterative rewrite's flat-cost guarantee is real correctness-versus-performance analysis, not a plug-and-chug exercise, and the dilemma survives regardless of which runtime is targeted -- and (2) the size of the blowout is not guessable from the premise alone: a student's naive intuition (recursion should cost 'a bit more' per call, not qualitatively change the outcome) is actively wrong, and the magnitude was only discoverable by actually computing both scenarios -- the case-research agent explicitly re-ran the analysis under the TCO-honoring counterfactual (case.json.balance.margin_note; RESEARCH_LOG.md) expecting the gap to collapse toward parity, and instead found it still blows past SPEC §2's ~20% cap at 50.8%, confirming the lopsidedness is structural (a genuine property of the real cited benchmarks, S1/S2) rather than an artifact of the Go/non-TCO modeling choice (MA7) that could be fixed by retargeting the runtime or retuning a Modeling Assumption. Per project owner: scoped narrowly to this case's own researched figures, not a general relaxation, and not retroactive to any other case.

modeling_assumptions.basis: Go is widely used for high-throughput metering/billing backends, and its compiler team has repeatedly and publicly declined to guarantee general tail-call optimization (S4) -- this supplies the case's real analytical fork.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: HIGH -- the single most dilemma-relevant modeling choice in the case. A TCO-honoring target runtime would collapse the cost gap toward the real ~2x Shallow-row ratio (S1) instead of the ~24x-to-6-million-times gap the TCO-not-honored columns show (S1, S2).

sensitivity_note: margin_pct (95.8%) is computed entirely from directly-measured Shallow-row data (S1) and is NOT itself a Modeling Assumption. But which Appendix D column that computation uses depends on MA7 (target runtime = Go). Under the TCO-honored counterfactual (a runtime that reliably applies TCO), the margin at the same Shallow row would be (0.333-0.164)/0.333 = 50.8% -- still well over the ~20% guideline. This case's margin is wide under either runtime choice; MA7 changes the size of the gap, not whether Option B wins on raw D4 numbers. See balance.margin_note.
